The brass railing was cold against Elias’s palms, a familiar chill that had seeped into his bones over forty years. Below, the Atlantic churned, a restless beast of black water and white foam, slamming against the granite teeth of the cliff. Inside the lantern room, the great Fresnel lens rotated with a hypnotic, rhythmic *click-whir, click-whir*, casting its sweeping beam across the dark expanse.

Elias wasn’t just a keeper; he was the guardian of a threshold. He had watched ships come and go, their lights like dying fireflies in the storm’s grip. He knew the moods of the sea better than he knew the lines of his own weathered face. Tonight, however, the silence was different. It wasn’t the absence of sound, but a heavy, waiting pressure. The barometer had dropped hours ago, and the wind carried the metallic tang of ozone.

A shadow detached itself from the darkness of the horizon. A vessel, small and unlit, drifted dangerously close to the jagged reef known as Devil’s Back. Elias didn’t hesitate.
